stories.title: Trump to meet President at Áras during visit next weekend
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is to meet President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin during his planned visit to Ireland next weekend. He is likely to arrive in Dublin early on the morning of Saturday 12 September, before travelling on Marine One helicopter to the Phoenix Park for meetings with Ms Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin. Mr Trump will spend Saturday night at his golf resort in Doonbeg for the Irish Open tournament. While a bilateral meeting with Mr Martin at Farmleigh House has long been expected, there had been doubt over whether the US President would meet President Connolly. It is understood that a draft itinerary for Mr Trump's visit early last month had no scheduled engagement at Áras an Uachtaráin, while a spokesperson for Ms Connolly had said she would consider any request for a meeting she received. President Connolly insisted during last year's election campaign that she would meet Mr Trump if the opportunity arose, but she was critical of his administration during her St Patrick’s Day message when she said that "the normalisation of war can never be accepted".

stories.title: HSE fined after records found covered in animal droppings
stories.summary: An investigation by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) into the storage of paper records by the Health Service Executive (HSE) has found incidents of documents contaminated by animal droppings, destroyed by mould, covered in rubble, or rotting due to water damage. Site inspections by DPC investigators found storage areas in states of "profound disarray and neglect", with records being stored in disused bathrooms, a shipping container in a turf shed, rooms without functioning lighting or heating, as well as derelict buildings. The DPC has imposed fines of €645,000 on the HSE for the breaches, and has also issued corrective orders. The investigation was launched in May 2024 after people gained access to two disused psychiatric hospitals and posted videos to social media showing boxes of medical records and patient files that were being stored in the vacant hospitals. The facilities in question were St Loman's Hospital in Mullingar, Co Westmeath, and St Conal’s Hospital in Letterkenny, Co Donegal. As part of its investigation, the DPC carried out-site inspections at 12 facilities across the country to establish if the cases highlighted on social media were isolated incidents or part of a systemic issue regarding the retention and storage of personal data contained in paper records, held by the HSE, in its external facilities.

stories.title: Central Bank urged to clarify Israeli bond position
stories.summary: The Central Bank is being urged to clarify whether responsibility for the approval of Israeli state bonds has reverted to Ireland after Luxembourg relinquished the role. Luxembourg has decided not to renew its authorisation of Israeli bonds since it expired as of midnight. Israel will now need another country to take on the role to bolster its ability to borrow through investors on European markets. Luxembourg held the role since September 2025. As a result, responsibility for the approval of Israeli bonds could revert to the Central Bank of Ireland, which had been designated the "home" state for this responsibility since the UK left the European Union. The Central Bank has declined to confirm whether it is assuming the role again, simply stating how the arrangement between Israel and the financial regulator of Luxembourg, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF), expired today. The Bank of Israel would have had to submit an application for its prospectus to Ireland by the end of August.

stories.title: Grafton's H1 profit rises on Ireland and Iberia growth
stories.summary: Grafton Group, which owns Woodie's DIY and Chadwicks here, today reported higher revenues and profits for the six months to the end of June and said that trading conditions are expected to remain broadly consistent for the rest of the year, Grafton, which also owns HSS Hire Ireland and Cygnum, said its revenues rose by 6.7% to £1.336 billion from £1.252 billion the same time last year. Adjusted profit before tax for the six months grew by 7.1% to £93m from £86.8m, while adjusted operating profit increased by 8.2% to £98.5m from £91m on the back of strong underlying trading and acquisitions in Iberia and on the Island of Ireland. The Grafton Board has declared an interim dividend of 11 pence per share, an increase of 2.3% on last year's interim dividend of 10.75 pence. The company said that strong performances on the Island of Ireland and in Iberia were driven by continued progress in executing organic and inorganic growth opportunities. But it added that challenging market conditions in Great Britain continue to weigh on profitability with market conditions expected to remain broadly consistent with those experienced in the first half of the year.

stories.title: Polish PM says fire at defence manufacturer was arson
stories.summary: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has described a fire at a defence manufacturer in Poland as "deliberate arson". The fire took place at the production plant of WB Group in the south-central Polish city of Skarżysko-Kamienna in the early hours of Monday morning and was extinguished by local fire crews after two hours. WB Group produces components for drone systems and the company's website states that the group started producing reconnaissance drones in Ukraine last year. Polish police and the country's Internal Security Agency are investigating the incident. Last Sunday, a large fire also damaged the warehouse of JFG Composites, a company in the eastern city of Lublin that produces components for the aviation industry. "As far as the fires in two plants in Lublin and in Skarżysko-Kamienna are concerned, in the case of Skarżysko-Kamienna there is no doubt that there was deliberate arson, that is, an act of sabotage," Mr Tusk told the media before a cabinet meeting in Warsaw this afternoon.

stories.title: Mickelson v Mná - a scan of past Irish Walker Cups
stories.summary: The Clare coast holds the attention of the golfing world this month. Doonbeg hosts the Irish Open for the first time, with the likes of Jon Rahm and Brooks Koepka part of the field. The owner of the resort is also planning to descend on the venue. Before that, Lahinch - where the aforementioned Rahm won the Irish Open in 2019 - becomes the third Irish links to host the Walker Cup. Offaly's Stuart Grehan, winner of the Amateur Championship in Royal Liverpool this summer and a one-time professional, is the only Irish player on the team this time. The two previous matches played in Ireland have failed to yield a British and Irish victory. The overall head-to-head is 40-9 and that's even after an uptick in British and Irish competitiveness in the last 35 years. After the 1987 match, the head-to-head was 28-2 to the Americans.

stories.title: O'Shea and McCarthy to stay on Ireland coaching ticket
stories.summary: The FAI have confirmed that John O'Shea, Paddy McCarthy and Gudmundur Hreidarsson have penned fresh deals to stay on Heimir Hallgrimsson's Republic of Ireland coaching ticket until the conclusion of Euro 2028. Following on from Hallgrimsson’s contract extension earlier this year, assistants O’Shea, McCarthy and Hreidarsson have all signed up to remain with the squad through to the 2028 UEFA European Championships, which are set to be hosted in Ireland and the UK. McCarthy will continue to balance his role with the national side alongside his coaching position at Crystal Palace. "I am honoured to extend my time with the national team," said O'Shea. "Having been involved with this group for several years, I have seen the immense progression and potential within the squad firsthand. Hallgrimsson aired his delight at nailing down the coaches, saying: "Since I arrived, John, Paddy, and Gummi have been an incredible support to me and integral to everything we are building here. Their knowledge of the players and the Irish game is invaluable. "I am delighted that we will continue to work together to drive this team forward and achieve the results our fans deserve."

stories.title: The Button Factory at 30 - keeping Dublin's music scene alive
stories.summary: At a time when hostility to Irish cultural venues sits at a peak, one Dublin haven remains intact. There's a general understanding that cultural institutions and venues tend to feel cold to the touch, only to become thawed by your attention. By contrast, everything within the Button Factory, which this year celebrates its third decade in business, has always felt warm. Inside, the four walls that frame it – lined with the names, awards and records it has helped, contributed to and encouraged – feel increasingly like refuge from a city that has spent the last ten years trading its artistic lineage for commercial prospects. Acting as a crucial bridge between the city we once knew and the one we’re now faced with, that it stands today at 30 feels less like an anniversary and more like a miracle. "People who come here have a certain amount of trust in the space," Finn McCarthy, venue coordinator at the Button Factory says. "Which tends to mean that whether you have a crowd of 550 or 185, the room feels full – even if that’s just of good will." Though the venue’s founding came in 1996, the story of the Button Factory – or Buttoner, for regulars – really starts in the 1980s. As Ireland reckoned a decade of recession, unemployment and emigration, Córas Iompair Éireann took it upon itself to buy a suite of dilapidated properties in Temple Bar to turn them into a central, underground bus station. As the plans were being drawn, the organisation offered available rooms as affordable, short term rentals to artists, creating unbeknownst to themselves something of a bohemian cultural hub. "Everyone was in a band in the 1980s, but no one had anywhere to practice or record," says Paddy Dunning, the Button Factory’s founder, and a former renter of the scheme. "So we built studios and rehearsal rooms from the things we could take for free from skips. Then, when we heard that the area was to be demolished to make a dirty, greasy bus station, we knew we had to do something." An alliance of 12, dubbed the Temple Bar Development Council, was quickly formed in an attempt to save the area. Together, they met with Paddy Teahon, then-assistant secretary of the Taoiseach's Department, and Charlie Haughey, then-Taoiseach, to share their belief of the area’s massive potential. Using Sheffield, a city which had recently been developed following the fall of the steel industry and had since become a cultural hub as a recent example, they managed to provide a convincing narrative. "As a result, we set up 23 cultural centres, saved many architecturally important buildings, created 1000s of jobs and saved hundreds of homes." While the area was being flipped, Dunning and his team moved their then-already well-respected studios, rehearsal spaces and storage – which had, at that stage, welcomed the likes of Van Morrison, Sinéad O’Connor and Spandau Ballet to record – to a space on Ormond Quay, where it thrived from 1991-95 as something of a community hub. "We had over 30,000sqft of rehearsal spaces, studios, cages for the bands and a 1000-capacity venue," Dunning says. "I still remember Louis Walsh calling me at the time to say he had no money but could this new band he was forming, called Boyzone, rehearse on credit." In 1996, the Temple Bar Music Centre was born, resplendent with an auditorium, rehearsal rooms, a college for sound engineering students and The Irish Rock 'n' Roll Museum Experience, with much of its stock donated personally from Philomena Lynott, mother of the legendary Thin Lizzy frontman Phil Lynott. Still, it arrived with compromise. "We had wanted more than what we got – a 1000-capacity venue instead of 600-capacity, 22 rehearsal rooms instead of seven – but we took what we got," Dunning says.

stories.title: Fontaines D.C. Slane tickets go on sale this morning
stories.summary: Tickets for Fontaines D.C.'s two concerts at Slane Castle next summer go on general sale at 10am on Thursday morning. The Dublin band will play the Co Meath venue on Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 June 2027, after a second date was added on Wednesday due to demand. Tickets are priced from €89.25, including booking fee and a €1 donation to Focus Ireland, and are subject to a 12.5% service charge per ticket, capped at €10.50. The shows will mark another major milestone for Fontaines D.C., who will become only the third Irish act to headline Slane Castle, following Thin Lizzy and U2. They will also become the first Irish act to headline the venue on consecutive nights. U2 played two sold-out concerts at Slane in 2001, but the shows were staged a week apart, on 25 August and 1 September.

stories.title: Conor Pope's tips for saving money at home this winter
stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. Additionally, the need to tumble dry clothes can be a big expense, alongside buying warmer clothing, extra food, and saving up for Christmas presents. "I've done the maths, and I reckon that winter time costs about €10,000 more for the average household than summer time," he states. "That's not even being wildly extravagant." The first step in bringing those costs down? Shopping around for an electricity provider. "The reality is that more than 70% of Irish consumers don't switch their energy provider," the savvy saver explains, "despite the fact that, even in a climate of rising prices, you can still knock about €500 off your annual bill - just by moving from company A to company B." Many people will avoid switching because it feels like too much hassle, but Pope insists that sites like Bonkers.ie and Switcher.ie make it incredibly straightforward.

stories.title: Enforcement of new e-scooter laws will be 'weak' - GRA
stories.summary: The President of the Garda Representative Association has said enforcement of new e-scooter laws due to come into effect tomorrow will be "weak". From tomorrow, the wearing of helmets and high-visibility clothing will be mandatory for those using e-scooters. Regulations are also being brought in to raise the minimum age for e-scooter use to 18 from 16, however this measure has had to be submitted to the European Commission after legal advice from the Attorney General's office. However, they probably will not be "any use whatsoever" against those determined to ignore the laws. "Enforcement on these laws is likely to be weak, for a multiplicity of reasons," he said. "Without registration of these vehicles, we really can't do anything with the user who speeds away or leaves a scene," he said.

stories.title: August saw end of 66-day partial drought in Co Carlow
stories.summary: The longest partial drought on record since 1941 concluded at the end of August, Met Éireann has said in its climate statement for the month. The partial drought in Oak Park, Co Carlow began on 20 June and lasted 66 days until 24 August. A partial drought is defined as a period of at least 29 consecutive days where the mean daily rainfall does not exceed 0.2mm. The previous longest partial drought was 62 days at Roches Point in Co Cork in the summer of 1983. August was "notably warm and drier than average for most of the month", Met Éireann said in its latest monthly climate statement. Mean air temperatures were above long-term averages from 1991 to 2020 across the country.

stories.title: McEntee aiming to 'further increase' defence spending
stories.summary: Minister for Defence Helen McEntee has defended Ireland's security spending in the face of repeated questions at the informal gathering of EU defence ministers in Co Wicklow. As part of Ireland's hosting of the Presidency of the European Council, the meeting was hosted by Ms McEntee, and chaired by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. There is an increased garda presence, road closures and airspace restrictions in the area for the meeting. Speaking at the conclusion of the meeting at Druids Glen resort, Ms McEntee acknowledged the underspend but insisted that was in the past. "I think we've been very clear in saying that in the past we have not spent as much or committed as much as we should have. But I believe that has changed, and that will continue to change. "We've increased our defence spending overall by 43% in the last few years alone.

stories.title: Service sector growth remains robust, employment stalls
stories.summary: Growth in the services sector remained robust in August on stronger new business, although employment in the sector registered no increase for only the fourth time in five and a half years, a survey showed today. The AIB S&P Global Services Purchasing Managers' Index inched up to 55.4 in August from 55.2 in July, remaining above the 50 level that separates growth from contraction by the clearest distance since November 2025. Strong growth in new business accelerated following a dip in activity earlier this year. While new export from abroad also rose, they did so at a more modest pace than in July. Sentiment among firms strengthened for the fifth successive month, with expectations for activity at the highest level in 18 months. Employment levels fell at the most marginal of rates following several months of rapid gains. Rising wage, fuel and transportation costs pushed cost inflation slightly higher, although it was well below the 40-month peak reached in April and May, and broadly in line with the long-run survey average.

stories.title: Nepal floods should mobilise climate action - UN
stories.summary: Nepal's flood disaster and Europe's wildfires should turn attention to the cost of climate change, the head of the world's biggest climate fund said in an interview. Mafalda Duarte, executive director of the UN's multi-billion-dollar Green Climate Fund, said many countries do not understand that the world faces tipping points from which it cannot go back. "We see globally climate change dropping in terms of priorities, with other things - conflicts and shocks - taking priority," she told AFP. "We see when there is will, that finance is mobilised to respond to emergencies. For some reason, we don't see the same type of response to climate - as if we can afford to wait." The Green Climate Fund was established by the UN to help developing countries deal with the impacts of climate change, and has invested $19 billion (€16.4 billion) across 134 developing countries. The US withdrew from the fund in January, and Britain halved its contribution in May.

stories.title: Knockout KO'd - Tyrone continue to go against the grain
stories.summary: Quiz question - name the two counties that still employ a straight knockout format in their senior men's football championship? You should get halfway there given the fame attached with Tyrone’s continued decision to ignore changing times - and the much-cited fact that no club has retained the title since Carrickmore all the way back in 2005. The action throws in tonight with the meeting of Ardboe and Edendork while Loughmacrory will be hoping to end that back-to-back hex when they meet Pomeroy on Saturday, but the fact of the matter is that if they’re not good enough then their title defence will be over at about 9pm this evening. The other county who still employs knockout football is less obvious, probably the last footballing county to come to mind. The Kilkenny senior championship is run off on a knockout format with Mullinavat getting the better of Tullogher-Rosbercon back in early May. The fact that the final was held so early in the season speaks volumes for where it stands in a ferociously hurling-dominated county, so it's truly the Red Hand County where the last bastion remains unconquered. Niall Gartland, a Tyrone-based journalist with the Ulster Herald, has covered approximately 30 club championship games a season for the last decade. He believes the knockout format is not a lifetime guarantee but, likewise, he sees no appetite currently for change.

stories.title: Transfers: Ogbene joins Lincoln on loan, Kenny to Preston
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland international Chiedozie Ogbene has joined Lincoln City on loan from Ipswich Town until January. The winger had spent last season on loan at Sheffield United and will once again return to the Championship with a Lincoln side promoted from League One last season. "This is a good opportunity and a great platform for myself to help the club, but the club can also help me," the Corkman told the Imps' club website after his temporary transfer was confirmed shortly before the deadline. "I’ve been around the Championship for a while, and I know it’s a physical league. We know how tough it can be and how it’s physically demanding." The move to Lincoln means Ogbene will link up with fellow Corkman Josh Honohan as well as another Ireland international in the shape of the on-loan striker Mason Melia. Preston North End have confirmed Ireland striker Johnny Kenny's arrival on a permanent deal from Celtic.

stories.title: Buttimer strikes again as Munster retain Interpro title
stories.summary: Beth Buttimer haunted Leinster once again as Munster held off their rivals to retain their Vodafone Women's Interprovincial Championship at Dexcom Stadium. Three weeks on from scoring four tries in her side’s 39-19 win against the same opposition, Buttimer scored two more in today’s final in Galway to make it back-to-back Interpro championships for Matt Brown’s side. The hooker’s first score on 20 minutes had given her side a slender 7-5 lead at half time, with Kathy Baker crossing for Leinster shortly before the break. And it would take until the 70-minute mark for either team to add to their total, as Buttimer touched down from the back of a rolling maul, before Enya Breen landed a high-pressure conversion which put her side nine points ahead, and crucially give them a two-score buffer heading into the closing minutes. The afternoon may well have come at some cost for Ireland head coach Scott Bemand, who saw second row Ruth Campbell limp out of the Leinster side in the opening half. Three weeks out from his team’s opening WXV Global Series game against USA in Tallaght, the Ireland head coach will also have some important decisions to make.

stories.title: Why Tupac's music and politics still resonate with the Irish
stories.summary: We present an extract from Words for My Comrades: A Political History of Tupac Shakur, the acclaimed book by Dean Van Nguyen. From Pitchfork and Guardian contributor Dean Van Nguyen comes a revelatory history of Tupac beyond his musical legend, as a radical son of the Black Panther Party whose political legacy still resonates today. stories.title: Would you use a €480 toothbrush that tracks your teeth using AI?
stories.summary: In the quest for greater health and wellness, many of us have already invested in gadgets like sleep and fitness trackers, as tech companies increasingly recognise the money to be made in creating tools to track and tweak our bodily habits. But is our growing fascination with 'healthmaxxing' a sign that there is an appetite for an AI-powered high-tech toothbrush? Dyson is certainly betting on it, as it launches its first-ever toothbrush: the Dyson CameraJet, a Wi-Fi-enabled toothbrush equipped with a camera and powered by AI. Known for their home appliances and haircare products, the launch marks Dyson's first foray into the wellness industry, and it brings with it a host of new and impressive ways to optimise a previously mundane task - and possibly frighten yourself in the process. Coming in at just shy of €500, it certainly promises a lot: the CameraJet cleans, flosses and even sprays tiny jets of mouthwash. Not only that, it takes 28 live images per second while brushing to identify and monitor gaps between teeth. For the morbidly curious, you can then connect the toothbrush to an app which will give the user a report and suggest fixes to improve your dental health.

stories.title: WMO warns El Niño could fuel extreme weather worldwide
stories.summary: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a potentially exceptional El Niño warming event is now firmly established in the tropical Pacific and is expected to strengthen significantly into a "very strong" El Niño over the coming months. The event could reshape rainfall and temperature patterns across large parts of the planet, increasing the risk of floods in some places, drought in others and additional extreme heat. The WMO says almost all land areas are likely to experience above-normal temperatures during the coming months. WMO forecasting centres put the probability of El Niño persisting through February 2027 at nearly 100%, a remarkable degree of certainty. It is the first time that an El Niño/La Niña update has been so unequivocal. The event is expected to continue intensifying through the autumn and peak towards the end of 2026, although its climatic effects are expected to continue well into 2027.

stories.title: Age measures not stopping underage social media access
stories.summary: There has been no reduction in underage children's access to social media platforms, despite legal obligations which came into effect in July 2025 designed to prevent this, according to a new report. The report, from online safety charity CyberSafeKids, found that despite new age-assurance measures, many eight to 12-year-olds still have accounts on 13+ social media apps. The research also shows that there has been a big increase in the use of generative AI among young people. It found that many children are continuing to encounter negative experiences online, with a significant increase in exposure to scams, bad or fake information. The report recognises the impact of collective parent movements in delaying smartphone ownership and social media access for primary school-aged children but, according to CyberSafeKids, there is clear evidence that it is not reaching every community equally. "The intense debate over banning under-16s from social media is missing the point," said CyberSafeKids CEO Alex Cooney.

stories.title: Burnham pledges to 'stick to Good Friday Agreement' as PM
stories.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to "stick 100% to the Good Friday Agreement" after he received criticism last week when he told the media that a referendum on a united Ireland was "off the table". During what was his first official visit to Northern Ireland, when he was asked by the media in Belfast whether he would be "the man at number 10 to press the button for a border poll", Mr Burnham said he was there "to listen and take a collaborative approach". "Some issues will be off the table, and that is one issue that will be off the table," he added, saying that he "wanted to focus on bringing people together". The remarks drew an angry response from nationalist politicians, with Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald stating that no prime minister has the right to "high-handedly" remove the provision for a unity referendum from the Good Friday Agreement. Asked about the comments in the House of Commons today, Mr Burnham said the purpose of his visit was "to get functional government in Stormont". SNP MP for Dundee Central Chris Law put to Mr Burnham that he "has no mandate to defy the constitutional wishes of the people of Northern Ireland, the people of Scotland or the people of Wales".

stories.title: McStay: New rule tweaks aimed at curbing slow attacks
stories.summary: For all the highs of the 2026 All-Ireland football championship, slow attacks and lateral play remain too prominent, according to Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG) chairman Kevin McStay. Mayo's historic triumph at GAA HQ capped a swashbuckling season, but the EAG have proposed a series of rule tweaks in the upcoming third level Division 1 league. The EAG was installed on the recommendation of the Football Review Committee (FRC) in their final report in 2025, charged with monitoring trends within the game following the sweeping rule changes launched in late 2024. Of the proposed nine changes which will be trialled in the Ryan Cup this year, the four-point goal, prohibiting the fisted point, the sixth substitute and the backcourt pass were highlighted by the FRC, but didn’t make it as far as recommendations. Limiting the number of consecutive handpasses allowable to three and modifying the kickout rule, requiring the ball to travel just 13 metres rather than beyond the 40m arc, are some of the other standout adjustments. "Before the championship was played, we were up and running," he said. "We took our lead from the FRC and what was left over from their report, to see if there was anything interesting in it, if there was anything we could do to further improve it.

stories.title: McDonald given permission to resume GAA club action
stories.summary: Mayo All-Ireland winner Kobe McDonald has been given the green light by AFL club St Kilda to play with his club Crossmolina for the remainder of their club championship campaign. The Deel Rovers side will be hoping to secure their spot in the knockout rounds when they face Mayo Gaels this weekend, and they should have their star youngster amongst their ranks. As reported by the Irish Examiner, McDonald, who had been given permission to remain with Mayo for the 2026 season after signing with the Melbourne club last November, and fellow Irish St Kilda players Eamonn Armstrong and Liam O'Connell will now line out with their clubs over the coming weeks. Armstrong plays with Duleek Bellewstown in Meath while O'Connell is a member of Ballincollig in Cork. McDonald headed to Australia days after Mayo’s famous All-Ireland final win over Kerry, but has been in Ireland recently and was on stage at Electric Picnic as members of the squad joined the Saw Doctors. "As a club, it's really important that we support our players in their lives outside of being professional AFL footballers," said Lenny Hayes, St Kilda's general manager of football.
